content: For instance, probabilistic risk assessments with quantified uncertainties can provide more detailed risk estimates. While this document provides a general means of assessing risks to these sensitive groups, additional chemical-specific information can significantly improve the accuracy of risk assessments, particularly for unborn and newborn babies. Another area of uncertainty is the risk assessment of bioaccumulative active ingredients, such as DDT, where chemical-specific data on metabolism and toxicokinetics are essential for accurate evaluation. Unintentional misuse, such as contaminated clothing, perspiration on the skin, or the use of contaminated rags, is challenging to account for in models and is often impossible to quantify. Situations involving misuse or accidents are generally not covered in this document. Reusing product containers is mentioned but not routinely modeled; however, this scenario can be addressed in specific cases and is more reliably quantified than most misuse situations. The model also does not account for the concurrent use of the same products for agricultural purposes. If the user of the model has knowledge of risky equipment or work patterns, it is strongly recommended to incorporate this case-dependent information as a source of default parameters. Similarly, the use of empty product packages to store food or drinking water is not addressed. However, chemical-specific or case-specific data should always be sought and used when possible. Anthropometric and physiological input parameters, such as weight, skin surface area, and ventilation rate, influence risk estimates, and ideally, data from the target population should be used. The database produced by the US Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) is extensive and up-to-date, covering all age groups and relevant anthropometric and physiological data points. It is also recommended for use by the HEEG and was used in this document. For body weight, the 25th percentiles are applied, and for respiration rate, HEEG recommendations are used. Drinking water consumption is estimated using USEPA 95th percentile values, as these products are typically used in tropical countries. When appropriate anthropometric data are available for the population being assessed, these should be used. Adult operators and residents are assumed to weigh 60 kg, while children, toddlers, and infants are assumed to weigh 20 kg, 10 kg, and 8 kg, respectively. In the guideline scenario, it is assumed that WHO recommendations and product label instructions are followed. In a lax standard scenario, no personal protective equipment (PPE) other than light clothing covering the trunk is assumed. Pesticide formulations commonly used in larviciding and mollusciciding include emulsifiable concentrates, wettable powders, granules, and other solid formulations. It is recommended to avoid treating water that could be used as drinking water for humans or domestic animals. Contamination of groundwater due to pesticides entering subsurface waters or improper disposal of used packages can be estimated when relevant. When larviciding involves spreading chemicals into water sources, it is crucial to assess the accessibility of these substances carefully and avoid using those that are dangerous to groundwater. Chemical-specific data should be available from registration data for estimating the concentration of contaminants in groundwater. Any valid, chemical-specific data available should be used.
